papers.title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
papers.abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

papers.title: Lower Bound for Region of Non-Distillable Magic States
papers.abstract: Magic states are a leading proposal for realizing fault-tolerant and universal quantum computation. At the present moment, much of the theory of magic states is not understood. Even simple questions such as what single qubit states have magic remain open. In Campbell and Browne's seminal paper on bound magic states, they prove the existence of states outside of the stabilizer octahedron which cannot be used to achieve universal computation. In this paper we expand upon their proof and determine a lower-bound on this region.

papers.title: Ancilla-free randomized Toffoli gates and the T-count of Boolean oracles
papers.abstract: In fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits, a Boolean oracle costs T gates and extra qubits, and on four or more qubits every exact Toffoli gate needs an extra qubit. Gosset, Kothari and Zhang showed that sampling a fresh random circuit for each call makes the T-count of the Toffoli gate independent of its size, but a direct implementation of their sampler uses about one extra qubit per bit of precision. We show that computing the sampled parities in place, on the gate's own controls, removes every extra qubit once the gate is large enough: each random circuit then uses about 8 T gates per bit of precision and borrows only the gate's own idle inputs. This is one T gate more per circuit than the best measurement-free variant that keeps one clean ancilla. The same holds for exclusive-ors of indicators of affine subspaces, such as equality tests and checks of linear equations. For randomized circuits that do not measure, this is within a factor of eight of optimal up to an additive constant, even with extra qubits, and when each random circuit computes a Boolean function exactly, closing the factor asymptotically is equivalent to determining the leading constant in the T-count of exact multi-controlled Toffoli gates. Finally, the oracle of the indicator of a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, while that of an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number, and extra qubits reduce the exponential cost only quadratically.

papers.title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
papers.abstract: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays. Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results: 1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill. 2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead. 3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{\Omega(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.

papers.title: Quantum Query Complexity of Tournament Solutions
papers.abstract: A tournament solution records a set of winners from a tournament, that is, from the outcomes of all pairwise comparisons among $N$ alternatives. We study the quantum query complexity of computing tournament solutions when the outcome of each comparison has to be learned by a query. Classically, the picture is uniform: the Copeland set, the uncovered set and the top cycle all require $\Theta(N^2)$ queries, and so does finding a single vertex of maximum out-degree. We show that the quantum query complexity of the top cycle can be computed with $\tilde\Theta(N)$ queries, and a Condorcet winner can be found with $\tilde \Theta(\sqrt N)$ queries. Finding a strong king requires $\Theta(N^{3/2})$ queries, the same as finding a vertex of maximum out-degree. We also give a self-contained alternative proof of the known $\Theta(N^{3/2})$ bound for finding a vertex of maximum degree, established by Gilani, Mande, Patro, and Raja. Our lower bounds reduce counting problems to tournament problems using Ambainis's adversary method. For the top cycle, we find a Hamiltonian path and locate the prefix forming the top cycle by divide and conquer.

papers.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

papers.title: On the Quantum Chromatic Gap II
papers.abstract: We confirm a conjecture of the first author [SODA'26] on a strong form of pseudo-telepathy for Khot's $d$-to-$1$ games: for every $d\geq 4$, every $\epsilon>0$, and every $k\in\mathbb N$, there is a $d$-to-$1$ label-cover game of classical value less than $\epsilon$ that admits a perfect quantum strategy using finite-dimensional shared entanglement with measurement contexts of radius at least $k$. As a consequence, there exist graphs whose quantum chromatic number $\chi_q$ is $3$ and whose classical chromatic number $\chi$ is arbitrarily large. This is the first improvement on the quantum chromatic gap since the work of Brassard, Cleve, and Tapp [Phys. Rev. Lett.'99], which produced graphs for which $\chi$ grows exponentially in $\chi_q$. To prove the conjecture, we proceed as follows. We start with a ``stretched'' version of the Mermin--Peres magic square, obtained by spacing out its equations and linking them with additional long equation wires. This operation increases the radius of the initial measurement contexts of a perfect quantum strategy for the game, while preserving classical unsatisfiability. We then apply parallel repetition to make the classical value small, and we turn the system into a pseudo-telepathic multi-layered Kneser hypergraph via a PCP construction of Dinur, Guruswami, Khot, and Regev [STOC'03]. Finally, we feed the resulting hypergraph into the reduction of Fei, Minzer, and Wang from hypergraph colouring to $4$-to-$1$ games, we establish quantum completeness of this reduction, and we show that it preserves context radius.

papers.title: What Can Be Computed with Indefinite Causal Structure?
papers.abstract: Can quantum computation become more powerful when operations do not need to follow a definite causal order? We study this question in the process matrix formalism of Oreshkov et al. (Nature Communications, 2012), which allows quantum operations to be connected without a fixed global order. In the computational model, a quantum circuit succinctly describes a process matrix, and the algorithm is given access to its generated channel, with computational cost measured by the size of the generating circuit. We give polynomial-time algorithms in two settings. First, general process matrix computation suffices to solve every problem in $\textbf{NP}$. The valid processes used by our algorithm satisfy the purification postulate of Ara\'{u}jo et al. (Quantum, 2017), and their generated channels are unitary, although their generating circuits are not. Second, requiring the process matrices themselves to be pure, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for unique-sink orientation, a general problem capturing several longstanding computational problems in optimization. Our unitary generators are constructed explicitly and efficiently. Assuming that unique-sink orientation has no quantum polynomial-time algorithm, our result shows that indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond $\textbf{BQP}$ within the process matrix formalism, even while preserving unitarity.

papers.title: GAnnET: A principled approach to automatically annotating charge stability diagrams
papers.abstract: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum-dot (QD) arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing. However, their large configuration spaces and inherent measurement noise make device tuning time consuming and difficult to scale. Although machine-learning (ML) approaches for automated tuning have proliferated rapidly, a fair comparison of methods remains limited by inconsistent metrics and a lack of standardized labeled datasets. Here, we introduce Geometry-Informed ANNotator for Electrostatic Topologies (GAnnET), a physics- and geometry-informed algorithm that automatically generates probabilistic state labels for charge stability diagrams (CSDs) of double-QD systems. GAnnET constructs local geometric models of CSD structure and combines them into a global state map with calibrated confidence, eliminating the need for manual annotation. We validate GAnnET on simulated and experimental CSDs and demonstrate consistent labeling suitable for ML training and benchmarking. By enabling reproducible annotation of experimental data, GAnnET supports community benchmarking and scalable automated QD operation.

papers.title: Latent Style-based Quantum Wasserstein GAN for Drug Design
papers.abstract: The development of new drugs is a time-consuming and expensive process, with average costs estimated to be up to around $2.5 billion. The first step in this process is the design of the new drug, for which de novo drug design, assisted by artificial intelligence, has blossomed in recent years and has revolutionized the field. In particular, generative artificial intelligence has delivered promising results in drug discovery and development, reducing costs and time to solution. However, classical generative models, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), can be difficult to train and are prone to mode collapse. Quantum computing may be an avenue to overcome some of these issues, providing compact models with far fewer trainable parameters, thereby enhancing the generalizability of GANs. We propose a new latent style-based quantum Wasserstein GAN (QGAN) for drug design, combining a variational autoencoder that maps molecular structures into a latent space with a hybrid quantum GAN. Our pipeline is benchmarked against classical models of the industry-relevant MOSES suite. Style-based noise reuploading at every rotational gate and a Wasserstein gradient penalty are used to improve trainability and to mitigate mode collapse. Training and large-scale sampling with circuits of up to 15 qubits are performed on noiseless quantum simulators to validate our architecture. We present an inference-only demonstration on an IBM Heron quantum computer using 5 qubits, sampling 2,500 new molecules, to investigate quantum noise effects. Our default QGAN, using 110 trainable generator parameters, reaches statistically comparable overall performance and statistically significant gains on selected drug-relevant metrics relative to both the MOSES classical latent GAN baseline, which contains about 700,000 trainable parameters for the generator, and a classical latent GAN with matched generator capacity.

papers.title: Learning unified control of intrinsic nonlinear spin dynamics in atomic qudits for magnetometry
papers.abstract: Generating and preserving metrologically useful quantum states is a central challenge in quantum-enhanced metrology. In low-field atomic magnetometry with multilevel atoms, the nonlinear Zeeman (NLZ) effect is both a resource and a limitation. It can generate internal spin squeezing within a single atomic qudit, but under fixed readout it also rotates and distorts the measurement-relevant quadrature, limiting the usable metrological gain. The problem is further complicated by the time dependence of both the squeezing axis and the nonlinear evolution itself. Here we show that reinforcement learning can transform NLZ dynamics from a source of readout degradation into a sustained metrological resource. Using only experimentally accessible low-order spin moments, a trained agent identifies a unified control policy for this class of intrinsically nonlinear sensing dynamics. We illustrate the approach in the \(f=21/2\) manifold of \(^{161}\mathrm{Dy}\), where the learned policy rapidly prepares strongly squeezed internal states and stabilizes more than \(4\,\mathrm{dB}\) of fixed-axis spin squeezing under continuous NLZ evolution. Including state-preparation overhead, the learned protocol yields a single-atom magnetic-field sensitivity of \(13.9\,\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\), approximately \(3\,\mathrm{dB}\) beyond the standard quantum limit. Our results establish learning-based control as an experimentally feasible route for converting unavoidable intrinsic nonlinear dynamics in multilevel atomic sensors into operational metrological advantage.

papers.title: A Unified Complexity Framework for Quantum Property Testing
papers.abstract: We develop a unified framework for analyzing the complexity of quantum property testing through functionals of the form $\mathcal{L}_{\phi}(\rho) = \operatorname{tr}(\phi(d\rho))/d$, where $\rho$ is an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state and $\phi$ is a given function. A master theorem is established that derives sample complexity lower bounds for estimating $\mathcal{L}_\phi(\rho)$ from properties of $\phi$, combining Haar-random moment encoding with moment matching and best polynomial approximation. Corresponding query complexity lower bounds follow from quantum sample-to-query lifting. The framework yields (nearly) tight bounds for a broad class of problems, including entropy estimation (von Neumann, R\'enyi, and Tsallis), closeness estimation (trace distance and Uhlmann fidelity), spectrum estimation, rank testing (operator rank, Schmidt rank, and matrix product states). In particular, combined with known upper bounds, we show that the sample complexity of von Neumann entropy estimation is \[ \Theta\!\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon\log^2(d)\max\{1, \varepsilon\log^2(d)\}} + \frac{\log^2(d)}{\varepsilon^2}\right), \] and the sample complexity of spectrum estimation is \[ \Theta\!\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log^2(d)\max\{1, \varepsilon^2\log^2(d)\}}\right). \] In summary, our results resolve several open problems and establish the optimality of 37 quantum algorithms since 2015, up to constant or polylogarithmic factors.

papers.title: Exact $T$-counts of CCZ layers from an isotropy bound
papers.abstract:
The $T$-count is a dominant cost of fault-tolerant Clifford$+T$ computation. We prove that every Hadamard-free Clifford$+T$ circuit with clean ancillas for a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates, the diagonal core of a parallel Toffoli layer, uses at least $6m+1$ $T$ gates. Campbell and Howard gave a circuit with $6m+1$, and to our knowledge this is the first proof that it is optimal for general $m$. The proof combines Campbell and Howard's self-orthogonality of the columns of the parity matrix with a rank (flattening) bound, sharpened by one. More generally, the argument gives a lower bound on the $T$-count of every diagonal gate in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, the isotropy floor, computable by Gaussian elimination. It is never below the stabilizer nullity $
u$ and reaches $2
u+1$ on non-Clifford gates whose phase is purely cubic. No bound that also holds for circuits with measurement and feedforward can do this, since such circuits implement CCZ ($
u=3$) with four $T$ gates and the layer with $4m$, where the floor gives seven and $6m+1$. The floor also recovers Campbell and Howard's count $4m+3$ for a fan-out of Toffolis. On the output of PyZX's TODD-based optimizer, relative to its Hadamard placement, it certifies $193$ of $311$ phase-polynomial blocks $T$-optimal once repeated parities are merged (at the best of five optimizer seeds), against $113$ for nullity, including $37$ of the $72$ blocks too large for exhaustive search.

papers.title: BAHAMAS: A Control Plane for Optimization and Execution of Variational Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) suffer from unstable optimization due to temporal noise drift and static qubit mappings that distort gradient signals across iterations. We present BAHAMAS, an online control framework that stabilizes noise exposure by adaptively selecting physical mappings via consensus-based fidelity estimation, without requiring simulators, offline training, or prior executions. Across real quantum devices, BAHAMAS improves optimization reliability and supports inference-time retargeting under drift through robust, per-iteration control.

papers.title: Barren Plateaus in Quantum Linear Combinations: Interference and Lie-Algebraic Control
papers.abstract: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal. We distinguish a single linear combination of unitaries (LCU) from a circuit that repeatedly alternates branch operations and ancilla mixing. For a single-pass LCU, independent branches with zero matrix means cannot erase the differentiated branch's gradient variance: the total variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. This bound holds at any gate position and does not require the circuit unitaries to be Haar-random. Beyond this lower bound, we derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify the additional contributions from interference between branches. One of these terms depends on relative coefficient phases and vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by $i \mathbb{I}$; a four-qubit matchgate example shows that it can be nonzero. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, we determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, including the available central phase directions. This control result predicts concentration only with additional assumptions on circuit sampling. Matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass LCU variances and exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. We also derive coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.

papers.title: SeQUeNCe.DQC: Full-stack Simulation of Distributed Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects multiple quantum processing units to overcome the scale limits of monolithic hardware. We introduce SeQUeNCe.DQC, a new top-level module within the SeQUeNCe package that compiles monolithic circuits into topology-aware execution plans and coordinates their execution using SeQUeNCe's existing quantum-network modules and protocols. We validate SeQUeNCe.DQC by reproducing a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation and comparing success probabilities with the reported 71% benchmark. We then evaluate how compiler strategy, topology, and memory capacity jointly govern distributed circuit execution time and success rate. In these experiments, our hybrid compilers successfully identified mixed TeleGate/TeleData execution plans that outperformed pure gate-teleportation strategies. By capturing the physical overhead of distributed quantum primitives, SeQUeNCe.DQC provides a rigorous platform for co-designing DQC software and hardware architectures.

papers.title: A quantum central path algorithm for linear optimization
papers.abstract: We propose a novel quantum algorithm for solving linear optimization problems by quantum-mechanical simulation of the central path. While interior point methods follow the central path with an iterative algorithm that works with successive linearizations of the perturbed KKT conditions, we perform a simulation working directly with the nonlinear complementarity equations. Using a two-stage quantum eigenpath traversal schedule, this approach yields an algorithm for solving linear optimization problems involving $m$ constraints and $n$ variables to $\varepsilon$-optimality using $\widetilde{O}\!\left((m+n)^{3/2}\,\varepsilon^{-1}+(m+n)^{1/2}\,\varepsilon^{-3/2}\right)$ queries to an oracle that evaluates a potential function. In the standard gate model (i.e., without access to quantum RAM), our algorithm can obtain $\varepsilon$-precise solutions to LO problems using at most $$\widetilde{O}\!\left(\left[\frac{(m+n)^{3/2}}{\varepsilon} + \frac{(m+n)^{1/2}}{\varepsilon^{3/2}}\right] \cdot \mathrm{nnz}(A)\right)$$ elementary gates, where $\mathrm{nnz}(A)$ is the total number of non-zero elements found in the constraint matrix.

papers.title: ShotQC: Reducing Sampling Overhead in Quantum Circuit Cutting
papers.abstract: The recently developed quantum circuit cutting technique greatly extends the capabilities of current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. However, it introduces substantial overhead in both classical postprocessing and quantum resources, as the postprocessing complexity and sampling cost scale exponentially with the number of circuit cuts. In this work, we propose an enhanced circuit cutting framework, ShotQC, which effectively reduces the sampling overhead through two key optimizations: shot distribution and cut parameterization. The former employs an adaptive Monte Carlo strategy to dynamically allocate more quantum shots to subcircuit configurations that contribute more to the variance in the final outcome. The latter exploits additional degrees of freedom in postprocessing to further suppress variance. Integrating these optimizations, ShotQC significantly reduces the sampling overhead without increasing classical postprocessing complexity, as demonstrated across a range of benchmark circuits.

papers.title: Quantum lower bounds for convex optimization and real matrix-vector query problems
papers.abstract: We (the author and the AI systems that did the heavy lifting) show that the quantum query complexity of minimizing a convex function over a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with evaluation and membership queries is $\tilde\Omega(n)$, nearly matching the best known upper bound. In particular, we show this even for quadratic minimization, which is equivalent to inverting an $n \times n$ real matrix using matrix-vector queries. We also show linear or nearly linear lower bounds on the quantum query complexity of computing the trace, the sign of the determinant, and the magnitude of the determinant of a real matrix in the matrix-vector query model. We use a novel quantum lower bound technique, the determinantal witness method, based on identifying a witness whose Fourier transform vanishes on low-rank matrices and that correlates well with the function being computed.

papers.title: Twisted Fourier Analysis of Quantum Weight Enumerators
papers.abstract: A unified Fourier framework for quantum weight enumerators of prime-power-dimensional qudits is developed in this paper. We introduce the notions of Weyl power spectrum and Weyl-conjugation autocorrelation for the Weyl-operator quantities nderlying the Shor--Laflamme weight enumerators. Representing these quantities as formal vectors, we show that they form a symplectic Fourier transform pair, from which the quantum MacWilliams identity follows by applying the Hamming-weight functional. This framework extends to a family of twisted Fourier transforms, including the Rains shadow transform. We show that identical-copy Bell sampling corresponds to a twisted autocorrelation related to the shadow enumerator through Weyl translation and Hamming projection. We further prove that all twisted Fourier transforms are Weyl translations of either the ordinary MacWilliams transform or the Rains shadow transform. This two-class reduction implies that the twists yield no additional independent coefficientwise positivity constraints under compatible projections. Nevertheless, the framework leads to refined MacWilliams and shadow identities that retain more Fourier information than ordinary Hamming weight enumerators. We employ these refined identities in linear programming, together with simplex mapping and shadow-coset counting, to exclude surviving candidate weight distributions. These techniques yield tighter bounds for binary and qutrit quantum codes, including nonexistence results for specific code parameters.

papers.title: Adaptive Local Measurements For Quantum Learning Can Exponentially Outperform Nonadaptive Global Measurements
papers.abstract: Can measurements chosen adaptively, in response to earlier outcomes, be exponentially more informative than measurements fixed in advance? In many quantum settings, adaptivity helps at most polynomially; known exponential advantages require coherent measurements across copies or restricted measurements. We show an exponential advantage measuring one copy at a time, with no quantum memory kept between state copies, even when the nonadaptive learner may perform arbitrary global measurements on each copy. We construct explicit families of multi-qubit states in which a scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables, with an auxiliary marker indicating which one. An adaptive protocol identifies the relevant observable and then measures it using only single-qubit measurements and one round of adaptation. At fixed accuracy, it needs logarithmically many copies as the qubit count grows, whereas every nonadaptive protocol needs exponentially many. The same mechanism yields an exponential gap in local asymptotic minimax mean squared error constants, tight up to the exponential base. The states are separable and classical in label-dependent product bases; no entanglement or other nonclassical correlations are required. The gap comes from measurement incompatibility: the candidate observables cannot be measured jointly, so a fixed measurement must divide its information budget among them, while adaptivity selects the informative one. Accordingly, the separation disappears when the candidate observables commute, and cannot occur with fully observed classical samples. Measurement incompatibility thus emerges as a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement and quantum memory, that classical feedback alone can exploit.

papers.title: Time-Switching Energy-Harvesting Quantum Relay-Assisted FSO Communication with Displaced Squeezed Signaling
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a quantum relay-assisted free-space optical (FSO) communication system in which a decode-and-forward relay is powered by time-switching optical energy harvesting and forwards the decoded information using displaced squeezed signaling (DSS). To obtain a physically con sistent description of turbulence-induced loss for non-classical signaling, each hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic chan nel whose random transmissivity follows a truncated Gamma Gamma law, i.e., the Gamma-Gamma irradiance conditioned on the physically admissible range of a transmittance. Under this channel, coherent states remain pure, whereas squeezed states are mapped to mixed Gaussian states. Under Helstrom-optimal detection, the average error of the coherent hop is derived in exact Laplace-series form. For the DSS hop, we derive the output states, a closed-form Gaussian fidelity with rigorous two sided bounds on the Helstrom error, and prove the existence of a loss-aware optimal photon partition. Furthermore, we prove that optimized squeezing preserves both the turbulence-induced diversity order and the leading asymptotic constant of coherent relaying, so that its benefit is a finite-photon-budget effect, and that an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction exists. A covariance-preserving benchmark with an exact series representation yields an analytical upper bound on the achievable throughput whose absolute gap vanishes as the relay photon budget grows. Numerical results based on the exact mixed-state Helstrom error quantify the benefit of squeezing and the regime in which it is useful.

papers.title: Automated Verification of Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing
papers.abstract: We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first fully automated verification framework for QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation. Our framework exploits the structure of the simulation algorithm: Hamiltonians are given as weighted sums of Pauli strings, embedded into larger unitaries through block encodings, and transformed into time-evolution operators by quantum signal processing (QSP). Using a symbolic Pauli-sum semantics for ancilla-indexed circuit blocks, our verifier proves that the distinguished all-zero ancilla block is proportional to the target Hamiltonian and infers the subnormalization factor automatically. It then verifies the QSP layer by extracting the implemented polynomial transformation and certifying its approximation error. This structure-aware abstraction is essential for scalability. Composing our verified block encoding and QSP wrapper yields an estimated macro-expanded size of about 1.52 million gates. The verifier certifies the block encoding once and checks the QSP layer through its abstract interface, without expanding the oracle calls. Our implementation verifies block encodings of structured Pauli-sum Hamiltonians with up to 256 system qubits and verifies QSP Hamiltonian-simulation instances by extracting their implemented polynomials and checking the resulting approximation bounds. These results show that fully automated verification can handle common Hamiltonian-simulation circuits at substantial scale when it exploits their algorithmic structure.

papers.title: Quantum communication: a discrimination approach
papers.abstract: We develop a state discrimination approach to unassisted quantum communication through a noisy quantum channel. Starting from the operational duality between entanglement recovery and state discrimination, we construct entanglement-generation codes with explicit decoders constructed from Petz recovery maps. The resulting error bounds hold for every number of channel uses and are expressed in terms of Petz-R\'enyi coherent information. For product sources, they yield exponential error decay at rates below coherent information.

papers.title: Classical communication over quantum channels: does entanglement help in nature?
papers.abstract: Can entangling codewords across independent uses of a quantum channel improve the rate of classical communication? An old conjecture states that there is no such entanglement advantage for all channels. Although Hastings's result and follow-up works disproved this conjecture, it turns out that enormous dimension is required to construct a channel where entanglement enhances classical communication. This indicates that there might be no entanglement advantage for many physical channels, or for all low dimensional channels. Motivated by recent progress on (generalized) amplitude damping channels, we propose a general Schur-weighted block entropy inequality, and show that there is no entanglement advantage for all phase-covariant channels including multi-level amplitude damping channels, generalized dephasing channels, and damping-dephasing channels. As a by-product, we also recover the recently established result that there is no entanglement advantage for all qubit channels.

papers.title: Quantum-inspired space-time PDE solver and dynamic mode decomposition
papers.abstract: The numerical solution of time-dependent PDEs posed over the combined space-time domain, instead of treating time sequentially, leads to space-time methods. Treating time as another spatial dimension allows parallelization across time and simultaneous adaptivity in spatial and temporal discretizations. However, space-time formulations suffer from the curse of dimensionality due to the (d+1)-dimensional domain. Time-series forecasting methods, such as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), also suffer the same scaling for storing and processing measurement data. In this work, we investigate whether quantum-inspired tensor network methods can mitigate this curse for both solving PDEs and data-driven modeling. We formulate a space-time matrix product state (MPS) encoding to represent either the space-time solution or time-series data. Using this representation, we develop a unified framework that combines an MPS space-time PDE solver with an MPS-DMD algorithm. We benchmark our MPS space-time solver for linear and nonlinear PDEs in both (1+1) and (2+1) dimensions, including non-diffusive regimes such as shockwave formation and Allen-Cahn phase separation. We observe that the MPS ansatz efficiently captures the spatio-temporal correlations of the solutions, with a 99% reduction in parameters with respect to the grid size. We demonstrate the MPS-DMD algorithm in two cases. First, the MPS space-time solver generates the MPS encoding of the time-series data. We then apply MPS-DMD directly to predict the dynamics without solving PDEs. Second, for the general case where data is available as dense arrays, MPS-DMD needs an intermediate compression step. We implement a streaming-like compression algorithm and observe a 97% reduction in memory, with MPS-DMD predictions matching those of exact DMD.

papers.title: Discovery of connectivity-trainability trade-off of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization
papers.abstract: Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits are promising candidates for near-term quantum computing due to the conjectured classical hardness of their sampling task and their shallow, highly parallelizable structure. Despite extensive studies of their complexity-theoretic properties, the role of circuit connectivity in their trainability as variational ansatze remains poorly understood. In this work, we present an investigation of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization that traces a mechanistic chain linking circuit connectivity, entanglement generation, and gradient scaling: increasing connectivity drives the circuit output toward Haar-like statistics and volume-law entanglement, and this increase in entanglement is consistently associated with an exponential decay of the gradient variance and degraded optimization performance, while sparser architectures retain stable gradients at the cost of global expressibility and entanglement capacity. This connectivity-entanglement-gradient mechanism produces a nontrivial connectivity-trainability trade-off, demonstrating that effective IQP-based Hamiltonian optimization requires a balance between global expressibility and trainability rather than maximal expressivity alone. In particular, on our benchmarks, a circuit generating no entanglement already matches the optimization performance of more highly connected circuits, and a circular topology retains entanglement capacity while preserving trainability, making it a broadly effective choice among the architectures considered.

papers.title: Scalable Message-Passing Quantum Graph Neural Networks in the Weisfeiler-Leman Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Graphs provide a natural language for relational data in chemistry, biology and optimisation. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have driven much of the recent progress in learning from such data through message passing, a single primitive that generalises convolution and attention. Quantum counterparts have been proposed, but with limited connection to message passing and few guarantees on performance or scalability. More broadly, the trainability of variational quantum circuits is a recognised bottleneck for their wide applicability, and pre-training has emerged as one way to address it. Yet for a quantum model to be useful, it must offer expressivity guarantees along with demonstrable scalability. Here we show how a quantum graph neural network can be built to perform message passing, to be permutation equivariant, and to sit at a chosen level of the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, the standard measure of how finely a model can tell graphs apart. We show that, as for classical GNNs, the training can be done first on small graph instances, allowing for a pre-training that can mitigate usual training issues, and its output can be read out at a cost that stays low as the graph grows. We validate the framework in large-scale simulations of up to 56 qubits across three datasets, on synthetic graphs that ordinary message passing cannot separate, on molecular property prediction, and on the travelling salesperson problem. Our framework opens a path for near-term quantum algorithms with theoretical guarantees and practical scalability, bringing the principles of graph learning into quantum circuit design.

papers.title: Depth-Efficient Quantum Topological Data Analysis for Regime-Specific Detection of Financial Stress
papers.abstract: We present, to our knowledge, the first adaptation of Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) to quantum topological data analysis, reformulating Betti number estimation as a depth-efficient variational optimization over a compressed qubit register. From a Takens embedding and Vietoris-Rips filtration of S&P 500 returns, we extract combinatorial Laplacians and recast null-space counting as a continuous-PCE Rayleigh-quotient minimization with variational deflation, encoding $n_k$ simplex indices into $O(n_k^{1/\kappa})$ qubits with shallow, ancilla-free circuits. Because the resulting loss is rational rather than bilinear in the correlators, the barren-plateau bound of Sciorilli et al. does not transfer; empirically the gradient variance decays only polynomially, with no exponential barren plateau, over $n=4$-$12$ qubits. The classical stage matches ripser on all 190 sliding windows (2003-2010). On the real market Laplacians ($\beta_1=1$-$22$), PCE-VQE recovers no null vector from a random start, but warm-starting from a classical null-space surrogate recovers $\beta_1$ exactly on all seven windows tested ($n_k \le 259$), placing the obstacle in the optimization landscape rather than the encoding. Chronologically split classification gives in-regime ROC AUC 0.818, but out-of-distribution evaluation on the 2020 COVID shock and 2022 rate cycle (AUC 0.009, 0.515) shows the calibration does not generalize across crisis regimes.

papers.title: QSoftCore: A Conceptual Foundation for Quantum Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) requires understanding application requirements, quantum programs and algorithms, quantum computation paradigms, executions, and deployment. However, relevant quantum computing (QC) concepts are often defined across physical, mathematical, and paradigm-specific levels of abstraction, making it difficult for the QSE community and hence proposed methods to refer to them consistently. To this end, we present QSoftCore, a conceptual model that reorganizes established QC concepts from a software engineering perspective and connects quantum applications, computational problems, algorithms, configurations, programs, and paradigm-specific computation specifications with state evolution, execution results, and backends. Our assessment against QSE literature across key software engineering activities indicates that QSoftCore provides shared QC referents for quantum computations, executions, deployment configurations, backends, and measurement evidence across the QSE lifecycle.
